idiom_name: named exports + semantic function names (module surface as the interface)
implementation_notes: With no static types, names are the whole runtime contract, so the discipline is applied at the module boundary: export named, self-describing functions (`estimateArrival(cart)`) instead of a default export carrying an object of `handle`/`doStuff` methods, and let the module name supply the context so names do not repeat it (`order.addLine(...)`, not `order.addOrderLine(...)`). JSDoc comments carry what a name cannot - parameter roles, thrown errors, `@returns` - and are the only documentation a package consumer sees; MDN's own guidance asks for concise, human-readable, semantic names and forbids Hungarian prefixes and type-in-name conventions. Keep the classic class-with-getters form only where the object genuinely owns mutable state and the accessor is a cheap property read; a `getX()` that computes, caches or fetches is where names start lying.
pitfalls: Without types nothing complains about `flag`, `data`, `res` or `obj`: enforce descriptive names with ESLint (`id-length`, `unicorn/prevent-abbreviations`, `naming-convention` in TypeScript) instead of trusting review.

A single default export hides the surface (`import api from './api'`), leaving callers to discover names by reading the file; named exports (or `export * as shipping from ...`) make the interface visible and statically checkable.
Renaming an export is a breaking change for every consumer; the `export { x as y }` alias looks like a fix but leaves two names for one concept in circulation.
